name: Liberal democracy
summary: A system of government that joins representative democracy with liberal constitutionalism: free, competitive elections with universal suffrage, legally equal citizens, protected civil and political rights, rule of law, and separated powers. It is usually paired with a market economy and private property, and leaves wide room for disagreement on welfare, taxation and social policy.
scope: The mainstream model described in political science (Dahl's polyarchy rights, Madison in Federalist 10, the UDHR) as practiced in Western-style democracies, whether republics or constitutional monarchies. Answers reflect what the system itself requires; policy questions it leaves open are marked neutral or low confidence. Excludes illiberal democracy and the electoral-only definition.

keyFigures.name: James Madison
keyFigures.role: Author of Federalist No. 10 and a framer of the US constitutional system of checks and representation.

keyFigures.name: John Locke
keyFigures.role: Philosopher of consent and rule of law whom Wikipedia credits for the rule-of-law tradition.

keyFigures.name: Robert Dahl
keyFigures.role: Political scientist who set out the eight rights of polyarchy used to define liberal democracy.

universal-healthcare.rationale: Liberal democracies range from universal public systems to insurance mixes, so the stance is inferred from the UDHR social-rights tradition and is contested between left and right adherents.

raise-minimum-wage.rationale: Adherents are split between left and right liberal-democratic parties; the system itself is indifferent to wage-setting.

markets-allocate-better.rationale: Wikipedia describes liberal democracies as market-based with protected private property, though many adherents accept substantial regulation.

public-ownership.rationale: Private property and a market economy are the norm in liberal democracy, though some publicly owned utilities exist in mainstream states.

tax-the-wealthy.rationale: Taxation levels are an ordinary partisan question inside liberal democracy, with no settled adherent position.

unions-good.rationale: Freedom to form organizations is one of Dahl's rights and the UDHR protects joining trade unions, so unions are broadly accepted though adherents differ on their weight.

property-fundamental.rationale: Private property is protected from state expropriation, and the UDHR bars arbitrary deprivation, but it is not "very hard to override" in most systems, so the answer is mild.

regulate-corporations.rationale: Regulation levels are a standard left-right dispute within liberal democracy.

cut-welfare.rationale: Mainstream adherents accept the welfare state in some form (UDHR Art. 22) while disputing its size; cutting it broadly is a minority view.

worker-ownership.rationale: Not a feature of the system, which keeps private ownership of firms; inferred from the market-economy precondition.

surveillance-ok.rationale: Adherents are split between security priorities and civil-liberty limits on state power.

legalize-drugs.rationale: Drug policy is not defined by the system; adherents across liberal and conservative parties differ.

restrict-hate-speech.rationale: Wikipedia lists hate-speech and Holocaust-denial restrictions among the limits many liberal democracies impose, though the United States model differs and critics say they go too far.

strong-leader.rationale: Separation of powers, rule of law and checks on executives run against leaders bypassing institutions.

state-harmful.rationale: Liberal democracy presupposes a constitutional state that protects rights and provides law; it is the opposite of anarchism.

limit-guns.rationale: Gun policy varies widely between liberal democracies and is split among adherents.

empower-police-military.rationale: A partisan question; the system itself calls for law-bound, accountable security forces rather than more or less funding.

legalize-sex-work.rationale: Policy differs across liberal democracies and adherents are divided between liberty and protection arguments.

decide-locally.rationale: Federalism is common and subsidiarity is valued, but unitary liberal democracies exist; no settled adherent view.

rehabilitation.rationale: Human-rights norms and the rule of law favor humane treatment, though adherents are split on punishment versus rehabilitation.

traditional-family.rationale: Genuinely split between conservative and liberal adherents; the system is neutral on family forms.

same-sex-marriage.rationale: Most liberal democracies have legalized it under equal-rights principles, though conservative adherents dissent.

abortion-legal.rationale: Split among adherents and legal regimes in liberal democracies vary.

more-religion-public.rationale: Freedom of religion and a neutral state are the norm, but some liberal democracies have state churches; inferred from general principles.

correct-racial-injustice.rationale: Equal rights without distinction (UDHR Art. 2) supports redress in principle, but remedies such as affirmative action are contested among adherents.

gender-social-construct.rationale: Not addressed by the system; adherents differ.

preserve-national-culture.rationale: Cultural policy is outside the system's definition and adherents differ between civic and cultural conceptions.

gradual-change.rationale: Liberal democracy channels change through constitutional procedure and elections, with peaceful transfer of power.

reduce-immigration.rationale: Immigration levels are a partisan question; the source describes populist restriction as a tension, not a defining position.

empower-international-orgs.rationale: Adherents differ on sovereignty versus international cooperation; the UDHR itself is an international instrument.

free-trade.rationale: Liberal democracies are associated with some trade restrictions, and adherents are split between free-trade and protectionist views.

nation-first.rationale: Split between internationalist and nationalist adherents.

humanitarian-intervention.rationale: Adherents are divided between human-rights interventionism and sovereignty or non-intervention.

open-borders.rationale: Mainstream liberal democracies maintain border controls, and the UDHR protects leaving a country, not entering one; open borders is a minority position.

limit-growth.rationale: Prosperity and a market economy are assumed in the model, but green adherents differ.

drastic-climate-action.rationale: Policy priority varies by party within liberal democracies.

tech-solves-problems.rationale: Not a position of the system; adherents are split.

expand-nuclear.rationale: A policy question on which adherents differ; nothing in the system speaks to it.

revolution-justified.rationale: The system relies on a loyal opposition accepting election results and peaceful change; the UDHR preamble allows rebellion only as a last resort against tyranny.

experts-over-public.rationale: Democratic authority rests on the will of the people (UDHR Art. 21), though the SEP notes representative systems and a division of labor with experts are accepted.

central-planning.rationale: Liberal democracy is described as market-based and capitalist with protected private property, which excludes central planning.

socialized-markets.rationale: Inferred from the private-property market model; worker or public ownership is not part of the system.

land-value-tax.rationale: A tax-policy idea unconnected to the system; adherents have no position.

basic-income.rationale: Adherents are split; the system is indifferent to this welfare design.

tariffs-protect-industry.rationale: Adherents are split between free-trade and protectionist parties.

state-directs-investment.rationale: The market model leaves investment mostly to private actors, though many democracies use industrial policy.

widespread-small-property.rationale: Wikipedia notes a significant middle class as a precondition, but widely spread ownership is not a stated aim.

abolish-money-wages.rationale: Money, wages and a market economy are assumed by the model.

abolish-central-banks.rationale: Not addressed; mainstream liberal democracies have central banks and only a libertarian fringe objects.

corporatist-bargaining.rationale: Competitive party politics and free associations are the model; state-recognized corporatist bodies are not, though neo-corporatist bargaining exists in some states.

one-party-rule.rationale: Multiple viable parties and competitive elections are defining.

monarchy-legitimate.rationale: Wikipedia lists constitutional monarchies among the forms liberal democracy takes, so a ceremonial monarch is accepted.

democracy-best.rationale: Democracy as the legitimate basis of government is the defining commitment, with majorities bound by rights.

direct-votes.rationale: The model is representative democracy; Madison argues representation refines opinion and direct democracy cannot control faction.

workers-councils.rationale: Parliamentary elected representation, not councils, is the basis of power.

right-to-secede.rationale: Not addressed; most liberal-democratic constitutions treat territorial integrity as settled, though some permit negotiated secession.

natural-rulers.rationale: Legal equality of citizens and the will of the people as the basis of authority exclude natural rulers.

political-violence-never.rationale: Peaceful procedure is the legitimate route, but the system allows state force and the UDHR preamble tolerates last-resort rebellion.

war-builds-character.rationale: Nothing in the model glorifies war; its norms of rights and peaceful competition run against this.

separate-church-state.rationale: Freedom of religion is core and most liberal democracies are secular, though some keep state churches, so the answer is moderate.

laws-from-scripture.rationale: Laws are grounded in the consent and equality of citizens, with freedom of conscience, rather than scripture.

private-courts-defense.rationale: Rule of law applied through public courts and an independent judiciary is a defining feature; the state keeps justice and defense.

military-superiority.rationale: A security-policy question on which adherents differ.

ethnic-nation.rationale: Citizens are legally equal regardless of ethnicity (universal suffrage regardless of ethnicity), which rejects ethnic definitions of the nation.

class-struggle-history.rationale: The model stresses competition and compromise among interests (Madison on factions) rather than class conflict as the driver of history.

equal-outcomes.rationale: Equality is legal and political; equal outcomes is not a goal, though welfare is accepted.

indigenous-land-authority.rationale: Not addressed by the system; liberal democracies differ and adherents are split.

colonial-reparations.rationale: Not a system position; adherents split.

civilizational-union.rationale: Inferred; the model describes states with their own constitutions, though regional unions like the EU have liberal-democratic support.

self-interest-moral.rationale: Madison treats self-interest as an unavoidable fact to be managed, not as a moral good; adherents differ.

duties-before-rights.rationale: Rights guaranteed to individuals are central, though the UDHR also notes duties to the community.

limit-population.rationale: Rights-based norms (UDHR family rights) oppose coercive population control, but nothing is stated directly.

industrial-civilization-disaster.rationale: The model assumes economic prosperity and a middle class as supports; the claim is a radical rejection of that.

accelerate-technology.rationale: Not an element of the system.

human-enhancement.rationale: Not addressed; split between liberty and precaution.

algorithmic-government.rationale: Authority rests on the will of the people and accountable elected officials, so handing decisions to algorithms is disfavored.

unbreakable-encryption.rationale: Split between civil-liberty and security adherents.

restore-past-order.rationale: Procedural change by election, with no stance on progress; inferred as mildly against restoration over progress.

results-over-ideology.rationale: Adherents split; pragmatism is common but the system is itself a set of principles.

direct-action.rationale: Change comes through elections and parliaments, with peaceful protest as a protected freedom rather than the main route.

means-match-ends.rationale: The emphasis on legitimate procedure supports aligning methods with aims, though the model does not state it as such.

return-to-foraging.rationale: Incompatible with the model of a state with law, markets and a middle class.

distribute-by-need.rationale: Market distribution is the norm, with welfare floors; distribution by need as the ultimate rule is a socialist aim.

production-for-use.rationale: Production for profit in markets is the model.

profit-exploitation.rationale: A Marxist claim; the model treats private profit as legitimate property income, and Wikipedia records Marxist criticism of it as external.

dictatorship-of-proletariat.rationale: Equal citizenship and competitive elections contradict class dictatorship.

collective-farming.rationale: Private property and individual ownership are the norm.

capitalism-causes-war.rationale: The model defends market capitalism; the claim is a Marxist critique, though some adherents hold left-liberal variants.

taxation-theft.rationale: The state taxes under law enacted by representatives; the claim is a libertarian one rejecting that.

harm-principle.rationale: The UDHR (Art. 29) permits limits on rights to protect others' rights, but also morality, public order and general welfare, so the harm principle is not strict.

individual-rights-only.rationale: Individual rights are central, but minority-protection and group measures are also used (SEP and Wikipedia); adherents differ.

conscription.rationale: Varies by country and adherents are split.

exit-over-voice.rationale: The vote and electoral accountability are the defining check on government, not exit; the UDHR affirms the right to leave but bases authority on the will of the people.

state-as-business.rationale: Government is accountable to citizens as members under law, not run as a firm.

positive-liberty.rationale: Adherents split between negative-liberty and welfare-liberal readings; the UDHR includes social rights.

media-academia-power.rationale: Elected officials hold democratic authority; the claim is a partisan critique, though it has a following on the right.

hereditarian-race.rationale: Equality of dignity and rights without distinction of race is stated in the UDHR.

organic-representation.rationale: Representation is through competitive parties and universal suffrage.

total-state.rationale: Limited, law-bound government and protected freedoms exclude a state directing every area of life.

national-rebirth.rationale: Radical rebirth is a revolutionary-nationalist theme at odds with constitutional procedure.

territorial-expansion.rationale: Rights norms and constitutional government do not endorse expansion; liberal democratic theory stresses self-determination.

personal-loyalty-rule.rationale: Authority rests on law and the will of the people, not oaths.

bound-labor.rationale: UDHR Art. 4 bars slavery and servitude; legal equality excludes bound labor.

no-neutral-knowledge.rationale: The SEP discusses epistemic arguments for democracy, which assume knowledge can be pursued by reasoning and information, though adherents are mixed.

universal-morality.rationale: The UDHR proclaims rights as universal across cultures, which is the claim's political form.

single-common-good.rationale: Madison's Federalist 10 treats interests as plural and to be balanced by institutions.

jewish-state-israel.rationale: Not addressed by the system; adherents split.

revive-national-language.rationale: A national-cultural question outside the system.

workplace-democracy.rationale: Democracy is the form of government, not of firms; inferred from the market and private-ownership model.

school-vouchers.rationale: Education policy is a partisan question; the UDHR requires free elementary education but not the model.

avoid-deficit-stimulus.rationale: Fiscal stance is a partisan question.

economic-freedom.rationale: Wikipedia treats economic freedoms and a market economy as preconditions of liberal democracy, following Lipset.

rule-by-example.rationale: Rule of law and written, public laws bind rulers, rather than moral example substituting for laws.

national-self-determination.rationale: Authority resting on the will of the people (UDHR Art. 21) supports self-governing peoples, though the system is about the form of government.

force-without-un.rationale: Adherents split between international-law and national-security views.

reason-over-faith.rationale: The system protects freedom of conscience and religion, so faith is not excluded; adherents differ.

welfare-for-citizens.rationale: A partisan question; the UDHR speaks of everyone, while states differ.

work-for-welfare.rationale: A partisan question within liberal democracy.

class-collaboration.rationale: Madison and the model favor balancing interests through institutions instead of class conflict.

sacrifice-heritage.rationale: Futurist claim at odds with the cultural freedoms and moderation of liberal democracy.

dominated-front.rationale: Not part of the model; liberal democracies are mostly the leading Western powers themselves.

workers-nation.rationale: Not addressed; the system rests on citizenship rather than class organization.

distinct-gender-roles.rationale: Legal equality of citizens and the UDHR's equal rights without distinction of sex.

ban-interest.rationale: A market economy with private lending is assumed.

racial-segregation-law.rationale: Equal rights before the law without distinction of race is a defining feature.

state-class-instrument.rationale: A Marxist thesis rejected by the model, in which the state is a legal framework answerable to all citizens.

assimilate-immigrants.rationale: Models of integration vary between multicultural and assimilationist liberal democracies.

elite-replacement.rationale: A conspiracy theory not part of the model; adherents reject it.

proportional-representation.rationale: Wikipedia describes both plurality and proportional systems as used in liberal democracies, with adherents split.

national-mission.rationale: Democracy promotion has adherents, but spreading one's government is not part of the model and conflicts with self-determination.

patriarchy-structural.rationale: Contested between progressive and conservative adherents.

political-elite-corrupt.rationale: The model assumes accountable representatives; the claim is a populist one that the SEP and Wikipedia identify as a challenge.

heritable-defect-limits.rationale: Violates rights to found a family (UDHR Art. 16) and legal equality.

security-forces-accountable.rationale: Rule of law applies to those who govern as well as the governed, so officials and forces can be held accountable.

night-watchman-state.rationale: Modern liberal democracies provide public services and welfare beyond minimal functions, though classical liberal adherents differ.

discourage-race-mixing.rationale: Contrary to legal equality and the UDHR right to marry without race restriction.

equal-moral-worth.rationale: The UDHR proclaims all born free and equal in dignity and rights, and liberal democracy has legally equal citizens.

socialism-one-country.rationale: A Marxist-Leninist debate; adherents have no position.

uniform-civil-code.rationale: Equal citizenship before the law supports common civil law, though some states permit personal-law accommodations.

restrict-conversion.rationale: UDHR Art. 18 protects the freedom to change one's religion.

ban-cattle-slaughter.rationale: Religious-based bans conflict with the secular and rights-based model.

no-religion-state-schools.rationale: Practice varies widely among liberal democracies.

state-strengthens-encirclement.rationale: A Marxist-Leninist doctrine contrary to limited government.

consent-of-governed.rationale: The will of the people as the basis of government authority (UDHR Art. 21) and Locke's consent tradition are central.

trade-surplus.rationale: Mercantilist aim; adherents mostly hold that trade need not be a contest, though some governments pursue surpluses.

population-transfer.rationale: Violates equal rights and the right to leave and return to one's country.

initiating-force-wrong.rationale: The state legitimately uses force under law; an absolute libertarian principle is not accepted.

competition-drives-progress.rationale: Competition between parties and firms is central, but social-Darwinist struggle between peoples is rejected; split.

ban-extremist-parties.rationale: Militant democracy is practiced in Germany and elsewhere, but its use is contested and the US follows a looser model, so moderate agreement.

freedom-as-non-domination.rationale: A republican theory not part of the standard liberal-democratic account; adherents split.

separated-powers.rationale: Separation of powers into branches with an independent judiciary is a defining structural feature.

vanguard-party.rationale: Multiple competing parties and elections are the model; a vanguard party is Leninist.

priority-to-poor.rationale: Adherents are split; the UDHR social rights support a floor, not priority.

right-to-buy-council-homes.rationale: The system leaves housing policy open; left and right adherents differ.

restrict-strikes-picketing.rationale: The UDHR protects forming and joining trade unions, but liberal democracies regulate strikes differently and adherents are split on how far.

population-causes-poverty.rationale: Not defined by the system; inferred from the UDHR's social-rights framing, which treats poverty as a matter of institutions and policy.

diversity-weakens-cohesion.rationale: Equal citizenship and protected rights regardless of descent are core features, and the system is built to manage pluralism, as Madison argued in Federalist 10.

offices-by-lottery.rationale: Representative government by election is a defining feature, and Madison preferred representation to direct democracy.

emergency-suspend-protections.rationale: Rule of law and protected rights are defining; militant democracy allows limited defensive measures, so some adherents accept narrow emergency powers.

price-controls-essentials.rationale: The system is usually paired with a market economy, though policy is left open and wartime controls have been accepted.

party-controls-media.rationale: Free expression and independent press are defining rights of liberal democracy.

party-commands-army.rationale: Civilian, constitutional control of the armed forces under the rule of law excludes party command.

long-naturalization-wait.rationale: The system leaves citizenship rules open and democracies differ on residence periods.

representatives-worker-pay.rationale: Nothing in the system requires it, and most liberal democracies pay officials well, but it is not ruled out.

party-discipline-binding.rationale: Free-mandate representation is the usual liberal-democratic norm, though party whips are common in practice.

pool-sovereignty.rationale: Many liberal democracies join pooled-sovereignty bodies, but the system does not require it, so adherents are split.

head-commands-forces.rationale: Separation of powers means the legislature, not the head of state alone, controls the government and military.

church-by-bishops.rationale: Religious freedom and a state neutral toward belief mean church governance is not for the state to set.

clerical-rule.rationale: Authority rests on popular consent and secular law, with no office reserved for clergy.

defeat-own-government-war.rationale: Citizens' duties to the state and the rule-of-law order run against working for its defeat.

censor-art-for-virtue.rationale: Freedom of expression is a core right, and moral-character censorship is the kind of restriction it excludes.

unlimited-reelection.rationale: Practice differs: the US limits presidents while parliamentary systems have no term limits, so the system is split.

recall-officials.rationale: Some liberal democracies allow recall and most rely on elections and impeachment; Madison favoured representation insulated from passing opinion.

notes: Many answers are neutral or low confidence because liberal democracy specifies a form of government, not a program on economic or social policy; most such questions split adherents along party lines.
